# Case study: coastal shipping flows on the map {#sec-m3-estudo-de-caso} In module 1 we arrived at an origin–destination matrix of coastal shipping in TKU. It was a table. Now it becomes a map. Along the way, it answers a question the table did not. > *Where, geographically, are the country's coastal shipping corridors; how much cargo (in > tonnes) do they carry; and what is the average distance travelled per tonne?* ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(sf) library(dplyr) library(stringr) library(ggplot2) library(readxl) crs_br <- 5880 # SIRGAS 2000 / Brazil Polyconic, for the national map ``` ::: ## Step 1: The municipal OD matrix ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} colunas <- c("ano", "perfil", "sh2", "pais_origem", "uf_origem", "cidade_origem", "instalacao_origem", "pais_destino", "uf_destino", "cidade_destino", "instalacao_destino", "tku") cabotagem <- readxl::read_excel("dados/cabotagem_tku_2025.xlsx", na = c("", "-")) stopifnot(ncol(cabotagem) == length(colunas)) names(cabotagem) <- colunas cabotagem <- cabotagem |> dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::where(is.character), str_squish)) |> dplyr::filter(tku > 0) |> dplyr::mutate( uf_origem = stringr::str_to_upper(uf_origem), uf_destino = stringr::str_to_upper(uf_destino), offshore = uf_origem == "ZEE/PLAT. CONTINENTAL", tku_bi = tku / 1e9 ) od <- cabotagem |> dplyr::summarise(tku = sum(tku), .by = c(offshore, uf_origem, cidade_origem, uf_destino, cidade_destino)) c(pares = nrow(od), tku_bi = round(sum(od$tku) / 1e9, 1)) #> pares tku_bi #> 428.0 286.9 ``` ::: ## Step 2: Coordinates from the municipality name Here is the bridge between module 1 (text standardisation and `join`) and module 2 (geometry). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} arquivo <- "dados/brutos/muni_br.gpkg" if (!file.exists(arquivo)) { br <- geobr::read_municipality(code_muni = "all", year = 2022, simplified = TRUE, showProgress = FALSE) sf::st_write(br, arquivo, quiet = TRUE) } muni <- sf::st_read(arquivo, quiet = TRUE) chave <- function(nome, uf) { paste( nome |> stringr::str_to_lower() |> stringi::stri_trans_general("Latin-ASCII") |> stringr::str_squish(), stringr::str_to_upper(uf), sep = "|" ) } centroides <- muni |> sf::st_point_on_surface() |> dplyr::mutate(k = chave(name_muni, abbrev_state)) |> dplyr::select(k, code_muni, name_muni, abbrev_state) nrow(centroides) #> [1] 5570 ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # diagnosis BEFORE the join: which ANTAQ municipalities do not exist in the IBGE boundaries? pontas <- dplyr::bind_rows( od |> dplyr::filter(!offshore) |> dplyr::transmute(k = chave(cidade_origem, uf_origem)), od |> dplyr::transmute(k = chave(cidade_destino, uf_destino)) ) |> dplyr::distinct() nao_encontrados <- pontas |> dplyr::anti_join(sf::st_drop_geometry(centroides), by = "k") nao_encontrados ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: If this table comes back empty, standardisation solved everything. When something appears, the usual causes are an old spelling of the municipality, a different accent or a facility registered in a neighbouring municipality. The fix is an explicit lookup table, never a silent adjustment. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} de_para <- data.frame( k_antaq = "santana do livramento|RS", k_ibge = "sant ana do livramento|RS" ) ``` ::: ### The offshore case The 37 links leaving the Exclusive Economic Zone have no municipality of origin. Ignoring them would erase 38% of the TKU (see @sec-m1-limpeza), so they get an **explicit origin at sea**: a representative point in the Campos Basin, where most of the production is. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ponto_zee <- sf::st_sfc(sf::st_point(c(-40.20, -22.40)), crs = 4674) origens <- od |> dplyr::mutate(k = dplyr::if_else(offshore, "zee", chave(cidade_origem, uf_origem))) coords_zee <- sf::st_sf( k = "zee", code_muni = NA_real_, name_muni = "ZEE / Plataforma Continental", abbrev_state = NA_character_, geom = ponto_zee ) pontos <- dplyr::bind_rows(centroides |> dplyr::rename(geom = geom), coords_zee) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-important} A single point for the whole EEZ is a **declared simplification**, not data. It serves to let the map communicate the maritime origin of the flow; it does not serve to compute actual navigation distance. Any number derived from this geometry must come with that caveat in the report. That is why, in step 5, we treat the distance with an explicit correction factor. ::: ## Step 3: Building the desire lines ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} xy <- sf::st_coordinates(pontos) idx <- setNames(seq_len(nrow(pontos)), pontos$k) od_geo <- origens |> dplyr::mutate( k_o = k, k_d = chave(cidade_destino, uf_destino), i_o = idx[k_o], i_d = idx[k_d] ) |> dplyr::filter(!is.na(i_o), !is.na(i_d)) c(pares_totais = nrow(origens), pares_com_geometria = nrow(od_geo), tku_preservado = round(sum(od_geo$tku) / sum(origens$tku), 3)) #> pares_totais pares_com_geometria tku_preservado #> 428.000 419.000 0.997 linhas <- sf::st_sf( od_geo, geometry = Map(\(a, b) sf::st_linestring(rbind(xy[a, ], xy[b, ])), od_geo$i_o, od_geo$i_d) |> sf::st_sfc(crs = 4674) ) |> dplyr::mutate(tku_bi = tku / 1e9) ``` ::: The `tku_preservado` (TKU preserved) line is the check that matters: if the value is not close to 1, part of the flow was left off the map for lack of a coordinate. The map would then tell a different story from the table. ## Step 4: The flow map ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} arquivo_uf <- "dados/brutos/uf_br.gpkg" if (!file.exists(arquivo_uf)) { ufs <- geobr::read_state(year = 2020, showProgress = FALSE) sf::st_write(ufs, arquivo_uf, quiet = TRUE) } ufs <- sf::st_read(arquivo_uf, quiet = TRUE) |> sf::st_transform(crs_br) top_linhas <- linhas |> dplyr::slice_max(tku_bi, n = 40) |> dplyr::arrange(tku_bi) |> sf::st_transform(crs_br) pontos_usados <- pontos |> dplyr::filter(k %in% c(top_linhas$k_o, top_linhas$k_d)) |> sf::st_transform(crs_br) ggplot() + geom_sf(data = ufs, fill = "grey97", colour = "grey86", linewidth = 0.2) + geom_sf(data = top_linhas, aes(linewidth = tku_bi, colour = offshore, alpha = tku_bi)) + geom_sf(data = pontos_usados, size = 0.9, colour = "grey25") + scale_linewidth_continuous(range = c(0.2, 3.2), name = "TKU (billion t·km)", transform = "sqrt") + scale_alpha_continuous(range = c(0.4, 0.9), guide = "none") + scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#1a5b8a", `TRUE` = "#b3402a"), labels = c(`FALSE` = "port to port", `TRUE` = "offshore (EEZ)"), name = NULL) + labs( title = "Coastal shipping: main flows in TKU, 2025", caption = paste("Source: ANTAQ, Estatístico Aquaviário (TB6.1).", "Straight lines between municipal centroids; offshore origin represented", "by a single point in the Campos Basin.") ) + theme_void(base_size = 10) + theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12), legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Coastal shipping flows in TKU (2025): the 40 largest municipal links](m3-06-estudo-de-caso_files/figure-html/fig-caso-fluxos-1.png){#fig-caso-fluxos width=1200} ::: ::: The `transform = "sqrt"` on the width is not an aesthetic detail: without it, the largest link (almost 28 billion t·km) would have a line dozens of times thicker than the median and would cover the whole coastline. ## Step 5: From TKU to tonnes The published data are TKU. Since TKU = tonnes × kilometres, knowing the distance we can estimate the tonnage. That is where geometry starts producing new information. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} linhas <- linhas |> dplyr::mutate( dist_reta_km = as.numeric(units::set_units(sf::st_length(geometry), km)), # navigation follows the coast: the real route is longer than the straight line. # 1.25 is an illustrative factor; in an official study, use nautical distances. dist_rota_km = dist_reta_km * 1.25, toneladas_est = tku / dist_rota_km ) linhas |> sf::st_drop_geometry() |> dplyr::summarise( tku_bi = sum(tku) / 1e9, toneladas_mi = sum(toneladas_est, na.rm = TRUE) / 1e6, distancia_media_km = sum(tku, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(toneladas_est, na.rm = TRUE) ) |> dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::everything(), \(x) round(x, 1))) |> knitr::kable() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | tku_bi| toneladas_mi| distancia_media_km| |------:|------------:|------------------:| | 286.1| Inf| 0| ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} linhas |> sf::st_drop_geometry() |> dplyr::slice_max(tku, n = 10) |> dplyr::transmute( origin = dplyr::if_else(offshore, "EEZ/Platform", paste0(cidade_origem, " (", uf_origem, ")")), destination = paste0(cidade_destino, " (", uf_destino, ")"), `TKU (bn)` = round(tku / 1e9, 2), `Dist. (km)` = round(dist_rota_km), `Tonnes (mn)` = round(toneladas_est / 1e6, 2) ) |> knitr::kable(align = "llrrr") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |origin |destination | TKU (bn)| Dist. (km)| Tonnes (mn)| |:--------------|:-------------------------|--------:|----------:|-----------:| |EEZ/Platform |São João da Barra (RJ) | 27.89| 145| 191.68| |EEZ/Platform |São Sebastião (SP) | 19.59| 726| 26.99| |EEZ/Platform |Angra dos Reis (RJ) | 17.42| 527| 33.06| |Juruti (PA) |São Luís (MA) | 16.47| 1656| 9.95| |EEZ/Platform |Madre de Deus (BA) | 15.28| 1358| 11.25| |Oriximiná (PA) |Barcarena (PA) | 10.48| 1258| 8.33| |EEZ/Platform |Osório (RS) | 8.38| 1632| 5.13| |Manaus (AM) |Guarujá (SP) | 8.33| 3526| 2.36| |EEZ/Platform |São Francisco do Sul (SC) | 8.16| 1197| 6.82| |EEZ/Platform |Ipojuca (PE) | 7.88| 2053| 3.84| ::: ::: ::: {.callout-warning} This number is an **estimate**, and the report must say so in a sentence: it depends on the assumed distance, which is the straight line corrected by a factor. For official tonnage data, ANTAQ itself publishes throughput in tonnes in its cargo tables. Comparing the estimate with the published figure is, by the way, an excellent validation exercise. ::: ## Step 6: Corridors ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} corredores <- linhas |> sf::st_drop_geometry() |> dplyr::mutate(corredor = dplyr::case_when( offshore ~ paste("Offshore →", uf_destino), TRUE ~ paste(uf_origem, "→", uf_destino) )) |> dplyr::summarise(tku_bi = sum(tku) / 1e9, toneladas_mi = sum(toneladas_est, na.rm = TRUE) / 1e6, ligacoes = dplyr::n(), .by = corredor) |> dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(tku_bi)) corredores |> dplyr::slice_head(n = 12) |> dplyr::mutate(part = tku_bi / sum(corredores$tku_bi), dplyr::across(c(tku_bi, toneladas_mi), \(x) round(x, 2)), part = scales::percent(part, accuracy = 0.1)) |> knitr::kable(align = "lrrrr") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |corredor | tku_bi| toneladas_mi| ligacoes| part| |:-------------|------:|------------:|--------:|-----:| |Offshore → RJ | 50.20| 236.24| 3| 17.5%| |PA → MA | 22.49| 13.26| 4| 7.9%| |Offshore → SP | 19.59| 26.99| 1| 6.8%| |Offshore → BA | 15.28| 11.26| 2| 5.3%| |AM → SP | 12.40| 3.52| 3| 4.3%| |PA → PA | 10.48| 8.33| 1| 3.7%| |SP → AM | 10.47| 3.02| 3| 3.7%| |Offshore → RS | 8.38| 5.13| 1| 2.9%| |Offshore → SC | 8.16| 6.82| 1| 2.9%| |Offshore → PE | 7.88| 3.84| 1| 2.8%| |RJ → AM | 4.90| 1.37| 3| 1.7%| |SC → CE | 4.29| 1.23| 4| 1.5%| ::: ::: ## Step 7: Export ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dir.create("resultados", showWarnings = FALSE) sf::st_write(sf::st_transform(linhas, 4674), "resultados/cabotagem_fluxos.gpkg", layer = "fluxos_od", delete_dsn = TRUE) writexl::write_xlsx( list("Corredores" = corredores, "Pares OD" = sf::st_drop_geometry(linhas)), "resultados/cabotagem_od_2025.xlsx" ) ``` ::: ## What this case study showed 1. The `join` by municipality name (the subject of module 1) is what connects a tabular dataset to a geographic one. Text standardisation is not fussiness: without it, the map loses flow. 2. The `tku_preservado` check is the habit that separates a correct map from a pretty one. 3. Every geometric simplification (one point for the EEZ, a straight line instead of a route, a distance correction factor) must be **written down**: in the code and in the map's caption. 4. With geometry, the published data (TKU) produce new information (estimated tonnes, average distance, corridors). That is exactly the kind of analysis that justifies the tool.
